extracted.intended_audience: funding agencies, academic institutions, journals/publishers, organizations that supply metrics, and individual researchers (including committees making hiring, promotion, and funding decisions)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of recommendations (the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, DORA) for improving how scientific research outputs are evaluated by funders, institutions, publishers, metric providers, and researchers, emphasizing assessment of research on its own merits rather than journal-based metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Journal Impact Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Journal Impact Factor has a number of well-documented deficiencies as a tool for research assessment, including: A) citation distributions within journals are highly skewed; B) the properties of the Journal Impact Factor are field-specific: it is a composite of multiple, highly diverse article types, including primary research papers and reviews; C) Journal Impact Factors can be manipulated (or “gamed”) by editorial policy; and D) data used to calculate the Journal Impact Factors are neither transparent nor openly available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why JIF is unsuitable as a primary parameter for comparing scientific output of individuals and institutions; frames the motivation for the recommendations that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — eliminate use of journal-based metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to eliminate the use of journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, in funding, appointment, and promotion considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overarching principle to be adopted by funding agencies and institutions: journal-based metrics should not substitute for assessment of individual research outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — assess research on its own merits
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to assess research on its own merits rather than on the basis of the journal in which the research is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for evaluators to focus on scientific content and impact of specific outputs instead of the venue of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — capitalize on online publication opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to capitalize on the opportunities provided by online publication (such as relaxing unnecessary limits on the number of words, figures, and references in articles, and exploring new indicators of significance and impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages rethinking article format constraints and developing richer indicators of impact that take advantage of digital publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Recommendation 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, as a surrogate measure of the quality of individual research articles, to assess an individual scientist’s contributions, or in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct, general prohibition against substituting journal-level metrics for article- or researcher-level evaluation across hiring, promotion, and funding contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: For funding agencies — Be explicit about criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the criteria used in evaluating the scientific productivity of grant applicants and clearly highlight, especially for early-stage investigators, that the scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding agencies should publish clear evaluation criteria and emphasize content over journal reputation; special attention to early-stage investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: For funding agencies — Consider all research outputs and broad impact measures
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of research assessment, consider the value and impact of all research outputs (including datasets and software) in addition to research publications, and consider a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators of research impact, such as influence on policy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should include non-article outputs and qualitative impact indicators (policy influence, practice), not just traditional publications or citation counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: For institutions — Be explicit about hiring/tenure/promotion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the criteria used to reach hiring, tenure, and promotion decisions, clearly highlighting, especially for early-stage investigators, that the scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should make decision criteria transparent and reinforce content-focused assessment, with consideration for early-career researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: For institutions — Consider all research outputs and broad impact measures
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of research assessment, consider the value and impact of all research outputs (including datasets and software) in addition to research publications, and consider a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators of research impact, such as influence on policy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional assessments should encompass datasets, software, and qualitative impacts as legitimate research outputs when evaluating researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: For publishers — Reduce emphasis on Journal Impact Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatly reduce emphasis on the journal impact factor as a promotional tool, ideally by ceasing to promote the impact factor or by presenting the metric in the context of a variety of journal-based metrics (e.g., 5-year impact factor, EigenFactor, SCImago, h-index, editorial and publication times, etc.) that provide a richer view of journal performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should stop using JIF as primary promotional metric or at minimum present it alongside multiple complementary metrics to provide context.

rubrics_metrics.name: For publishers — Provide article-level metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make available a range of article-level metrics to encourage a shift toward assessment based on the scientific content of an article rather than publication metrics of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article-level indicators should be provided to allow assessment of individual articles’ influence and content, supporting evaluation beyond journal reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For publishers — Encourage responsible authorship and contribution information
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage responsible authorship practices and the provision of information about the specific contributions of each author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should adopt policies that require or promote clear attribution of individual author contributions to improve transparency and credit allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For publishers — Remove reuse limitations on reference lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal is open-access or subscription-based, remove all reuse limitations on reference lists in research articles and make them available under the Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference lists should be openly reusable to facilitate discovery, analysis, and transparency; publishers should license them openly regardless of access model.

rubrics_metrics.name: For publishers — Remove or reduce constraints on references and mandate primary literature citation where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or reduce the constraints on the number of references in research articles, and, where appropriate, mandate the citation of primary literature in favor of reviews in order to give credit to the group(s) who first reported a finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages giving credit to primary sources and avoiding arbitrary limits on references that can skew citation practices toward reviews instead of original reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: For organizations that supply metrics — Openness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open and transparent by providing data and methods used to calculate all metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric providers should disclose underlying data and calculation methods to allow scrutiny and reproducibility of metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: For organizations that supply metrics — Provide data under permissive licence and computational access
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the data under a licence that allows unrestricted reuse, and provide computational access to data, where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metric data can be reused and programmatically accessed to enable independent analyses and integration into other tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: For organizations that supply metrics — Define and combat inappropriate manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear that inappropriate manipulation of metrics will not be tolerated; be explicit about what constitutes inappropriate manipulation and what measures will be taken to combat this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric suppliers should define gaming behaviors and state enforcement or mitigation measures to preserve metric integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: For organizations that supply metrics — Account for article types and subject-area variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the variation in article types (e.g., reviews versus research articles), and in different subject areas when metrics are used, aggregated, or compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics and comparisons must adjust for differences across article types and disciplines to avoid misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: For researchers — Assess on scientific content in decision committees
rubrics_metrics.description: When involved in committees making decisions about funding, hiring, tenure, or promotion, make assessments based on scientific content rather than publication metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers serving as evaluators should prioritize content-focused evaluation and resist reliance on journal-level metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: For researchers — Cite primary literature where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever appropriate, cite primary literature in which observations are first reported rather than reviews in order to give credit where credit is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual researchers should prefer citing original reports to ensure proper attribution and credit distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: For researchers — Use a range of article metrics and indicators in supporting statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a range of article metrics and indicators on personal/supporting statements, as evidence of the impact of individual published articles and other research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting impact evidence (e.g., CVs, statements), include diverse article-level indicators and relevant outputs (datasets, software) rather than relying on journal reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For researchers — Challenge inappropriate assessment practices and teach best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge research assessment practices that rely inappropriately on Journal Impact Factors and promote and teach best practice that focuses on the value and influence of specific research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should advocate for reform, educate peers and committees, and promote assessment practices centered on specific research contributions.
